ann_115.text: Through this part, capital gains from 0 to 6849 US dollars clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 62% to about 46%.
This part reads only capital gains.

ann_116.text: Through this part, being older (22 to 58 years) clearly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 62% to about 81%, which offsets part of the drop with age elsewhere in the model.

It adds to the predicted chance only once age rises above about 50 years: going from 17 to 63 years clearly raises it from about 62% to about 88% for the typical person, and 8545 of 39009 training people are past that age.

This part acts on 8609 of 39073 training people, 5807 of whom have an income of $50,000 or less; for the typical person it acts on (a 57-year-old White married man born in the United States, a high-school graduate at level 9 on the 1-16 scale, an executive or manager in the private sector working 40 hours a week), it clearly raises the predicted chance from about 31% to about 50%.
For people born in Colombia the model clearly keeps the prediction above 99% at every age.
Being born in Colombia by itself raises it to above 99% through this part (on the training data only).

ann_117.text: Through this part, other service work clearly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 62% to about 72%.
In the training data, 3916 people work in other service jobs.

ann_118.text: Through this part, administrative or clerical work raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 62% to about 70% (on the training data only).
In the training data, 4481 people work in administrative or clerical jobs.

ann_119.text: Through this part, handling or cleaning work and not living in a family each change a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less only slightly (on the training data only).
In the training data, 1683 people are handlers or cleaners and 10067 do not live in a family.

ann_120.text: Through this part, not living in a family clearly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 62% to about 37%.

It acts on the 10067 people not living in a family among 39073 training people, 9086 of whom have an income of $50,000 or less; for the typical one (a 35-year-old White never-married man born in the United States, a high-school graduate in a professional job in the private sector, working 40 hours a week), it slightly lowers the predicted chance from about 98% to about 94%.

ann_121.text: Through this part, a missing occupation clearly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 62% to about 80%.

It acts on 2197 people with a missing occupation among 39073 training people, 1992 of whom have an income of $50,000 or less; for the typical one (a 33-year-old White never-married man born in the United States, a child of the household with some college at level 9 on the 1-16 scale, missing work class, working 36 hours a week), it slightly raises the predicted chance, which stays at about 99%.
A missing country of birth slightly lowers it for that person, staying at about 99% (on the training data only).

Through this part, a missing country of birth raises it from about 62% to about 72% for people whose occupation is recorded, but slightly the other way, from about 80% to about 72%, for people whose occupation is missing.

ann_122.text: Through this part, being born in Portugal lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 62% to about 18% (on the training data only).
In the training data, 49 people were born in Portugal.

ann_123.text: Switching this part off makes no difference to the predictions.

ann_124.text: Across the whole model, a higher education level (7 to 13 on the 1-16 scale), capital gains (0 to 6849 US dollars), capital losses (0 to 1887 US dollars) and older age (22 to 58 years) clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from about 84% to about 34%, from about 62% to about 14%, from about 62% to about 31% and from about 81% to about 52%.

Being a household member other than husband, wife, unmarried or not in a family clearly raises it to about 90%, not being married to about 87%, farming or fishing to about 85%, other service work or being married with the spouse absent to about 84%, and being a woman to about 73%.
Being a wife rather than a husband clearly lowers it to about 39%, being married to a member of the armed forces to about 46%, and working longer hours (24 to 55 a week) from about 70% to about 54%.

Being born in Colombia raises it to above 99% and in Trinidad and Tobago to about 92%, while being born in Portugal lowers it to about 27%, in Ireland to about 37%, and 5th-6th or 7th-8th grade as the highest education to about 30% and 41% (on the training data only).
Being born in Scotland raises it to about 81% and in Honduras lowers it to about 52% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this: only 16 and 14 people).

ann_115.original: SUPPORTED: affine relay. 1870 = ReLU(0.439*capital-gain + 0.850) never clips on train, so it is a linear rescaling of capital-gain that adds -0.702*cg - 1.359 to the logit and steepens the direct capital-gain term (-1.841) to a total slope of -2.54 per SD. No nonlinearity is used on the data domain (the knot sits at cg z = -1.94, below the data minimum -0.147). EVIDENCE: Always active on train (pre-activation in [0.786, 6.636], 39,073/39,073 rows), so on the data domain 1870 = 0.439*cg + 0.850 exactly and its logit contribution is -0.702*cg - 1.359 (range [-10.61, -1.26], SD 0.70). Combined with the direct edge (-1.841), the total capital-gain slope is -2.54 logit per SD, pushing toward class 0 (the 24% minority, presumably >50K). line_plot on train (39,073 rows): exit vs capital-gain correlation 1.000 (exactly linear over the observed range); 91.6% of rows sit at the zero-gain floor (cg z = -0.147). Mean-ablation of 1870 (replace by train mean): acc 0.8558->0.8553, AUC 0.9099->0.9093 (small, because the direct edge carries the same signal).
ann_115.proposed: This part clearly lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less as capital gains rise, from about 62% to about 46% at 6849 US dollars.

ann_116.original: SUPPORTED: a single-knot age hinge giving a U-shaped (in class-1 logit) age effect. Below age z~0.80 the direct age term dominates (class-1 logit falls with age, i.e. the high-income share rises); above the knot 4647 reverses the slope to +0.65 per SD, so older workers drift back toward class 1, matching the empirical rate (minimum P(y=1) ~0.60 near z 0.8). native-country:4 (64 rows, standardized value 24.7) rides on the same unit as a large class-1 offset (memorisation of a rare category). EVIDENCE: Knot (for rows not in native-country:4, where nc4 = -0.041) at age z = 0.798. Active for 21.9% of those rows. Net age effect on logit = -0.881*age + 1.224*ReLU(1.249*age + 0.711*nc4 - 0.968): slope -0.881 below the knot and +0.648 above it. Logit contribution range [0, 24.36], SD 1.00 (the largest hidden-node contribution). The 64 native-country:4 rows (value 24.69) have 4647 ~ 16.6 (+20 logit), i.e. they are forced to class 1. line_plot on train (39,073 rows): exit 0 below z~0.8 then linear; scatter exit range [0, 19.9] (the top from nc4 rows). Local binned net age effect (non-nc4 rows): z=-1.5: +1.31, z=-1: +0.88, z=0: -0.02, z=0.5: -0.44, z=0.8: -0.67 (minimum), z=1.5: -0.26, z=2: +0.07, z=3: +0.73. Empirical P(y=1) follows the same U: 0.999, 0.944, 0.664, 0.606, 0.597, 0.662, 0.764, 0.816. Mean-ablation of 4647: acc 0.8558->0.8436, AUC 0.9099->0.9009 (largest hidden-node effect).
ann_116.proposed: This part clearly raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less once age rises above about 50 years, partly offsetting the overall drop with age.

ann_117.original: SUPPORTED: a category offset for occupation:8 implemented by redundant relays. 1303 and 9258 never clip (affine); 2114 is dead on the whole input domain. Net effect: +0.45 logit for occupation:8 rows (via 1303) on top of the direct occupation:8 term; 9258 and 2114 are inert (excess structure). EVIDENCE: occupation:8 is binary (-0.334 / 2.996). 1303 takes only {1.711, 2.120} and 9258 only {0.240, 3.140} (always active, affine). 2114 pre-activation is 0.224*1303 - 0.886 in [-0.503, -0.412] so 2114 is dead on every possible input value of occupation:8, not just on train. Net logit: constant +1.878 plus +0.449 for occupation:8 rows (via 1303), +0.004 via 9258. line_plot on train (39,073 rows): exit-1303 vs occupation:8 correlation 1.000. Mean-ablation of 1303: acc 0.8558->0.8554, AUC 0.9099->0.9097; 2114: no change; 9258: max logit change 0.004.
ann_117.proposed: This part clearly raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less for other service workers, from about 62% to about 72%.

ann_118.original: SUPPORTED: occupation:1 receives a small positive class-1 offset (+0.37 logit) via the affine relay 4973; the parallel indicator 3119 is nearly inert (readout -0.0047). occupation:1 has no direct edge to the output, so this leaf is its only route. EVIDENCE: occupation:1 binary (-0.360 / 2.778). 4973 in {0.555, 2.400}, always active (affine). 3119 is 0 for non-occ1 rows and 2.349 for occ1 rows (a true indicator) but its readout is -0.0047 (max logit change 0.011). Net logit: +0.111 baseline and +0.368 for occupation:1 rows. line_plot on train (39,073 rows): correlation 1.000 (two-level step). Mean-ablation: 4973 acc 0.8558->0.8552, AUC 0.9099->0.9095; 3119 negligible (AUC unchanged).
ann_118.proposed: This part raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less for administrative or clerical workers, from about 62% to about 70% (on the training data only).

ann_119.original: SUPPORTED but near-inert: formally an occupation:6 x relationship:1 interaction gate (off only for relationship:1 rows outside occupation:6), but readout 0.0186 makes it worth at most +0.10 logit. It is a vestigial interaction, not a meaningful part of the decision. EVIDENCE: Four train levels: -1.011 (relationship:1 rows outside occupation:6, 9,693 rows, gate off), 0.074 (neither, 27,697), 4.164 (occ6 and rel1, 374), 5.249 (occ6 not rel1, 1,309). Logit contribution range [0, 0.098], SD 0.019. line_plot on train (39,073 rows): exit vs first entry correlation 0.995. Mean-ablation: acc 0.8558->0.8557, AUC unchanged at 4 d.p. (max logit change 0.093).
ann_119.proposed: This part changes the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less only slightly, for handlers or cleaners and people not living in a family (on the training data only).

ann_120.original: SUPPORTED: a category indicator for relationship:1 (-1.03 logit). Because the other relationship one-hots enter linearly and standardized one-hots shift every row, this indicator places relationship:1 between relationship:0 and relationship:4 on the class-1 logit scale. It is a lookup, not an interaction. EVIDENCE: relationship:1 binary (-0.589 / 1.697). 7530 = 0 for the 29,006 non-rel1 rows and 2.466 for the 10,067 rel1 rows: a pure indicator, -1.030 logit for relationship:1. relationship:1 has no direct edge to the output, so the net relationship effect for rel1 rows (sum of all relationship terms) is -0.14, vs -0.81 for relationship:0, +0.90 for 2 and 3, +0.18 for 4, -1.75 for 5. line_plot on train (39,073 rows): two-level step, correlation 1.000. Mean-ablation: acc 0.8558->0.8533, AUC 0.9099->0.9073 (second-largest hidden effect).
ann_120.proposed: This part clearly lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less for people who do not live in a family, from about 62% to about 37% for the typical person.

ann_121.original: SUPPORTED: an AND-NOT gate: +0.92 class-1 logit for occupation:0 workers, cancelled when native-country:0 is set (34 rows). occupation:0 has no direct edge, so this is its only route; the native-country:0 veto touches very few rows and is probably fitted noise. EVIDENCE: Train cells: occupation:0 & not native-country:0: 2,197 rows, 392 = 2.749 (+0.919 logit); occupation:0 & native-country:0: 34 rows, 0; not occupation:0: 0 regardless (36,842 rows). P(y=1) in those cells: 0.907, 0.853, ~0.75. line_plot on train (39,073 rows) along native-country:0 is near-flat (correlation -0.03) because the gate depends on occupation:0; the cell table above is the operative evidence.
